section.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
section.sectionRationale: Chapters 4 and 5 are one continuous vision, but the scroll now supplies the throne room with its drama and its crisis. No one is found worthy to open it, John weeps, and then a Lion is announced who turns out to be a slaughtered Lamb. This is the christological hinge of Revelation's opening vision, the moment the whole book pivots from the settled throne to the Lamb who alone can unseal history, so it stands as its own unit before the seals begin to break in chapter 6.
section.thesis: No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth is found worthy to open the scroll of God's purposes until the Lion of Judah appears, and He is a Lamb who was slain; His blood-bought worthiness turns John's weeping into an ever-widening chorus of worship that sweeps from four living creatures and elders to countless angels to every creature in creation.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the sealed scroll and the search for one worthy to open it; the Lion who is a Lamb, standing as though slain, taking the scroll; the new song, celebrating His ransomed and reigning people; and the song swelling outward into a universal doxology to the Lamb and the One on the throne.

units.label: The sealed scroll and the search for one worthy

verses.text: Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals.
And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?”
But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it.
And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it.

units.label: The Lion who is a Lamb

verses.text: Then one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the {{rhiza|Root of David}}, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals.”

Then I saw a {{arnion|Lamb}} who appeared to have been {{sphazo|slain}}, standing in the center of the throne, encircled by the four living creatures and the elders. The Lamb had seven horns and seven eyes, which represent the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth.
And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne.

When He had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.

And they sang a new song: “{{axios|Worthy}} are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You {{agorazo|purchased}} for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.
You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth.”

units.label: The doxology of all creation
units.note: to Him and to the Lamb

verses.text: Then I looked, and I heard the voices of many angels and living creatures and elders encircling the throne, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands.
In a loud voice they were saying: “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!”
And the four living creatures said, “Amen,” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

rhiza.gloss: Root. The Root of David draws on Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10, where a shoot rises from Jesse's stump and the nations rally to it. Christ is not only David's descendant, his branch, but also his root, the source of David's line and kingship, present before and greater than the king He descends from.

arnion.gloss: Little lamb, a diminutive form John uses twenty-eight times in Revelation as his favorite title for Christ. It carries the tenderness of a young, vulnerable lamb even while this Lamb bears seven horns of full divine power and receives the worship of all creation, holding together weakness and majesty in one figure.

sphazo.gloss: To slaughter, to slay violently, the verb used of sacrificial victims. The Lamb stands alive yet bears the marks of having been sphazo, slaughtered, a permanent reminder in heaven's throne room that His worthiness rests on a real, bloody death, not a symbol of one.

axios.gloss: Worthy, deserving. In chapter 4 the Creator was declared axios because He made all things. Here the Lamb is declared axios on different but equal grounds, because He was slain and by His blood purchased a people, so that creation and redemption together ground the praise of heaven.

agorazo.gloss: To buy in the marketplace, to purchase or ransom. The Lamb's blood is the purchase price for a people drawn from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation, language that recalls a slave market and casts redemption as a real, costly transaction that changes ownership from sin and the beast to God.

basic.context: John sees a scroll in God's right hand, sealed shut, and a search begins for someone worthy to open it. No one in all creation qualifies, and John weeps bitterly. Then an elder announces the Lion of Judah has triumphed, but when John looks he sees not a lion but a Lamb, bearing the marks of slaughter, standing at the very center of the throne. This Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts in an ever widening song of worship that spreads from the throne's inner circle to countless angels to every creature everywhere.
basic.hermeneutics: The scroll pictures God's sealed plan for history, judgment and redemption bound together, and the crisis is that plan cannot go forward until someone worthy comes to enact it. People debate exactly what the scroll contains and why reigning 'upon the earth' in verse 10 is sometimes translated as a present reality and sometimes as a future hope, but the passage's clear center is unmistakable: Jesus is worthy, and He is worthy specifically because He was slain.
basic.originalLanguages: John's favorite name for Christ here is arnion, a little lamb, used again and again through Revelation, a word that holds together vulnerability and the seven horns of full power. The Lamb was sphazo, slaughtered, real sacrificial language, and by that blood He has agorazo, purchased, a people for God. The elders declare Him axios, worthy, on the ground of that costly purchase, the same word used of the Creator in chapter 4, now applied to the Redeemer.
basic.typology: The Lion of Judah fulfills Jacob's blessing over his son in Genesis 49, and the Root of David fulfills Isaiah's promise of a shoot from Jesse's line that the nations would seek. The Lamb who was slain fulfills every sacrificial lamb of Israel's worship, especially the Passover lamb whose blood spared God's people from judgment. And the purchased kingdom of priests fulfills God's promise at Sinai that Israel would be a kingdom of priests to Him.
basic.christ: Christ is announced as the conquering Lion but revealed as the slaughtered Lamb, holding together in one figure the triumph of a king and the humility of a sacrifice. He alone is worthy to unseal God's purposes for history because His victory was won at the cross. He receives the same worship given to the One on the throne, an early and unmistakable declaration of His full deity, and He is the one whose blood forms a redeemed people into a kingdom and priesthood.
basic.god: God holds history's scroll in His right hand, but He does not act alone; He has purposed from eternity that His Son, the slain Lamb, would be the one to unseal His plan. The Father who is worthy as Creator in chapter 4 is joined here by the Son who is equally worthy as Redeemer, and all creation is drawn into worshiping them together, a picture of the shared, undivided glory of God.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 49:9-10 gives the first promise of the Lion of Judah's scepter. Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10 promise the Root of David, a shoot the nations will seek. Exodus 19:6 first calls Israel a kingdom of priests, now fulfilled in the Lamb's purchased people. Revelation 1:5-6 already anticipated this, praising Christ who freed us by His blood and made us a kingdom and priests.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible has been building toward one question: who can be found worthy to carry out God's purposes for a broken world? Here the answer arrives, not a conquering general but a slaughtered Lamb, and the ancient promises of a Lion from Judah and a Root of David converge on Him. His blood purchases a people from every nation, and all creation joins its voice to declare Him worthy, the climax toward which every earlier promise of a rescuer was pointing.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 is the second half of a single scene begun in chapter 4, and it is built as a drama in three movements: a crisis (verses 1 to 4), a reversal (verses 5 to 7), and a widening response (verses 8 to 14). The crisis is stated three times. The angel asks who is worthy, verse 2. The narrator says no one was able, verse 3. John weeps because no one was found worthy, verse 4. The pile of 'no one' sets up the reversal, which is announced in a single word, 'Behold.'

The reversal has an ear and an eye. John hears an elder announce a Lion, the Root of David, and then, when he turns to see, he sees a Lamb. The vision does not replace the announcement. It interprets it. What John hears is the triumph and what he sees is the way the triumph was won.

The response grows in size and number, and the structure of the worship is carefully arranged. First the creatures and elders, with harps and bowls of incense, sing a new song, verses 8 to 10. Then the voices of many angels add a sevenfold ascription, verses 11 and 12. Then every creature in the whole of creation, 'in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea,' joins in a fourfold praise to both the One on the throne and the Lamb, verse 13. The creatures say 'Amen,' and the elders fall down, verse 14.

The chapter also has a clear link back to the letters. The verb that is used of Christ in verse 5, 'has triumphed,' is the same verb as the one translated 'overcomes' in every letter and in 3:21, where He said 'just as I overcame.' Chapter 5 shows how He overcame.
context.historical:
John's hearers knew what a sealed document was. In the Roman world a will or deed could be sealed by witnesses, and the seals protected the contents until the proper person broke them. Some interpreters see an allusion to a will, in which the heir alone may open it, and others to a double document of the kind Jeremiah describes, which has a sealed copy and an open copy, Jeremiah 32:10-14. The scroll in verse 1 is written on both sides, which is unusual in the ancient world, where scrolls were normally written on one side, and the details suggest that it is full and complete.

The titles of verse 5 come from Jewish messianic hope. A contemporary Jewish apocalypse, 4 Ezra, describes a lion who is the Messiah from David's line, so the elder's announcement of a Lion from Judah would have sounded like the kind of deliverer many in Judaism were expecting: a warrior from David's house who conquers Israel's enemies. That makes the sight of a slaughtered Lamb more striking.

The Lamb itself spoke to every part of worship that the first hearers knew. They knew the Passover lamb, the daily lamb of the morning and evening offering, the lamb of Isaiah 53:7 led to slaughter, and John the Baptist's cry, 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29. The churches of Asia lived in a world in which power was displayed by conquest and a conqueror was shown as an eagle or a lion. A slain lamb at the centre of heaven's throne was a strange emblem to set against that.

The call of verse 9, 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' would also have been heard against the background of the empire. Rome claimed to rule all peoples. Here the true people of every nation are bought by the blood of someone else.
context.canonical:
The Lion of the tribe of Judah comes from Jacob's blessing, Genesis 49:9-10, where Judah is a young lion and the scepter does not depart from him until the one to whom it belongs comes. The Root of David is from Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10, where a shoot comes from Jesse's stump and the Root of Jesse stands as a banner for the nations. In Revelation 22:16 Jesus says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David.'

The scroll is related to Ezekiel's scroll with writing on the front and back, Ezekiel 2:9-10, and to the sealed scroll of Isaiah 29:11 and the sealed book of Daniel 12:4, which is shut up until the time of the end. In Revelation the seal is broken at last, and what was sealed in Daniel is opened by the Lamb.

The Lamb draws on the whole line of sacrificial lambs. Abraham said that God would provide the lamb, Genesis 22:8. The Passover lamb's blood turned judgment aside, Exodus 12:13. Isaiah saw a servant 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7. Peter says believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19.

The song that calls the redeemed 'a kingdom and priests' recalls Exodus 19:5-6 and is repeated in Revelation 1:5-6, and Peter says the same of the church, 1 Peter 2:9. The Lamb's place in the middle of the throne is taken up in Revelation 7:9-10, 14:1-4 and 22:1-3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John means to reveal how God's plan for history is carried out, and by whom. The scroll cannot be opened by power, by wisdom or by any creature's merit. The only one who can open it is one who died. The scene was written to tell persecuted Christians that the cross, which looked like defeat to Rome and might have looked like defeat to them, is the place from which the world is ruled.

He also intends to teach them how to read the rest of the book. Every later scene of conflict, judgment and victory is to be seen in the light of the Lamb who was slain. The warrior in chapter 19 wears a robe dipped in blood, Revelation 19:13, and the saints in chapter 12 overcome 'by the blood of the Lamb,' Revelation 12:11. The way of the Lamb is the way of those who follow Him, and John wants the churches to know that faithful suffering is not a detour from victory but a share in His.

The chapter is also meant to evoke worship. It ends not with a lesson but with a chorus that spreads to the ends of creation. The reader is meant to join it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a vision, and it describes what John saw: a scroll, a Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes, harps and bowls of incense, a chorus of myriads. It does not prescribe harps in church or demand that believers imagine a lamb with horns. The images belong to the language of vision, where horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

What carries over is the content of the song. The church sings what heaven sings: that the Lamb is worthy because He was slain and has purchased a people for God from every nation. The song is a pattern for the content of worship, in which the cross is central and praise is addressed both to the Father and to the Son.

The promise that the redeemed 'will reign upon the earth' describes the destiny of God's people. It should not be taken as a mandate for believers to seize earthly power in the present. The Lamb's own way to the throne was by the cross, and those who follow Him are called to the same road.

debates.question: Why is Christ announced as a conquering Lion but revealed as a slaughtered Lamb?

views.label: The Lamb reinterprets the Lion
views.case: John hears the language of military triumph, the Lion of Judah has 'triumphed,' but when he looks he sees a Lamb bearing the marks of slaughter, showing that Christ's conquest was accomplished precisely through His sacrificial death, not despite it; the cross is the victory, not merely a prelude to a separate future victory.

views.label: Both images hold together as complementary truths
views.case: Revelation elsewhere pictures Christ as a warrior king with a sword from His mouth and a name of Faithful and True; the Lion and Lamb titles are not in tension but describe one person from two true angles, His authority to judge and reign, and the sacrificial ground on which that authority rests.

debates.bearing: Either way, the passage refuses to separate Christ's kingship from His cross; His right to rule and to unseal history's judgments is inseparable from His having been slain, so worship of His power and worship of His sacrifice are one and the same act.

debates.question: Does 'they will reign upon the earth' in verse 10 describe a present reality or a future hope?

views.label: A present, already unfolding reign
views.case: Some manuscripts and translations render this as a present tense, 'they reign,' fitting Revelation 1:6 where believers are already called a kingdom now, and Christ's own present session at God's right hand, so redeemed believers already share in Christ's authority in some measure before His return.

views.label: A future reign yet to be consummated
views.case: Other manuscripts and most translations render it as future, 'they will reign,' fitting the larger pattern in Revelation where the saints' full reign with Christ over the earth awaits His return and the new creation, described later in Revelation 20:6 and 22:5.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the purchased people of the Lamb are destined to reign with Him; the manuscript question over the verb tense affects only whether that reign is already begun in seed form or belongs entirely to the age to come.

debates.question: What is the sealed scroll?

views.label: God's plan for judgment and redemption
views.case: The scroll is held in God's right hand and its seals are broken one by one in chapters 6 to 8, producing the events that unfold through the rest of the book. The scroll is therefore the programme of history, and only the Lamb can set it in motion.

views.label: A deed of inheritance, or the book of life
views.case: Some see the document as a will or title deed, which the rightful heir alone may open, and the double writing as marking a full legal document. Others link it with the Lamb's book of life, Revelation 13:8, since the Lamb's purchase is the ground of its opening.

views.label: The Old Testament promises now unsealed
views.case: Daniel 12:4 sealed the words until the time of the end, and Isaiah 29:11 speaks of a vision sealed up. On this view the scroll holds the promises that Scripture had left unfulfilled, and the Lamb is the one who opens them by fulfilling them.

debates.bearing: The three readings share a centre: the scroll is God's and the only one who can open it is the Lamb. The details of its contents matter less in the passage than the identity of the one who takes it.

debates.question: Do the redeemed reign now or later?

views.label: A future reign at Christ's return
views.case: The Greek verb in verse 10 is future in the best reading, 'they will reign,' and the BSB follows it. Later chapters speak of the saints reigning with Christ in a future kingdom, Revelation 20:6, after the beast has been defeated.

views.label: A present reign in Christ's reign now
views.case: The manuscripts vary between a present and a future, and the footnote notes the variant. The Lamb has already conquered, verse 5, and the church is already called a kingdom, Revelation 1:6, so the reign of the saints is begun in His reign and finished at the end.

debates.bearing: Everyone agrees that the reign of the saints rests on the Lamb's victory, and that it is finally realised in the new creation. The disagreement is about how much of it is present now.

study.originalLanguages:
The scroll is a biblion, a small scroll or book. It is 'written inside and on the back' (gegrammenon esothen kai opisthen) and katesphragismenon, sealed up, a perfect participle with the preposition kata that adds the sense of fully or completely, so that it has been sealed and remains so. Seven is the number of completeness, and so the document is perfectly secured.

The question 'Who is worthy?' sets the strong angel's voice against a silence that the narrative then describes in the imperfect: no one 'was able' (edynato), and John 'kept on weeping' (eklaion). The elder's command is a present imperative, me klaie, 'stop weeping.' Then comes enikesen, 'he conquered,' an aorist, the same verb nikao that is rendered 'overcomes' in each letter. The announcement says it as a past fact. The conquest has already happened.

The Lamb is arnion, a diminutive that appears about thirty times in Revelation and in the rest of the New Testament only once, in John 21:15, where it is used of the lambs Peter is told to feed. For the sacrificial lamb, other writers use amnos, as in John 1:29 and 1 Peter 1:19. John chooses a word that sounds small and vulnerable and then sets it among images of power.

The Lamb is hos esphagmenon, 'as though slaughtered,' a perfect participle again, and it stands beside the perfect hestekos, 'standing.' A slain Lamb stands. The perfect tense says that the slaughter has a lasting effect: the marks remain, though He lives. The seven horns and seven eyes explain themselves, for John says the eyes are the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth. The picture draws on Zechariah 4:10, where the seven eyes of the LORD range over the whole earth.

In verse 7 the Greek says that He 'came' and 'has taken' the scroll, using a perfect, eilephen, which gives the moment a lasting weight, and the text is spare about it: He simply takes the scroll from the hand of the One on the throne.

The new song is ode kaine, and kainos usually means new in kind or quality. The ground of the song is that 'You were slain (esphages) and by Your blood You purchased (egorasas) for God.' The second verb, from agora, the marketplace, speaks of buying, and the buyer here is the Lamb, with blood as the price. The list 'tribe, tongue, people, nation' is the first of several fourfold lists in Revelation, whose order varies from passage to passage, as in 7:9 and 14:6, which suggests the order is not the point; the point is that no kind of person is left out.

The ascription of verse 12 is made of seven words, power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory and blessing, all governed by a single article in the Greek, so that they are received as one gift. It stands beside the threefold praise of God in 4:11 and the fourfold praise of verse 13. The last word, 'Amen,' is said by the four creatures. It echoes the title of Christ in 3:14, who is the Amen.

typology.fulfillment: Jacob's blessing pictured Judah as a young lion that none dares rouse, with the scepter held until the one to whom it belongs comes. The elder uses the picture to announce the victory. The escalation is a reversal: the Lion's conquest is carried out as a Lamb's sacrifice. The correspondence to Genesis 49 is real, since Christ holds the ruler's scepter and the allegiance of the nations, but the way He wins is not what Israel imagined. The type is only partly adequate, for the lion alone would suggest that Christ conquers by force, while the vision shows that He conquers by being slain.

typology.type: The shoot and Root of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah saw a Branch growing from the stump of Jesse, a line that seemed cut down, and promised that the Root of Jesse would stand as a banner for the peoples, so that the nations would seek Him. Revelation says that this has happened in Christ, the Root and Offspring of David, Revelation 22:16. The nations that seek Him are the ones whom He has purchased from every tribe and tongue. The correspondence is exact in its direction, since the king who rose from a stump draws all nations to Himself. What Isaiah saw from afar is now seen at the throne.

The Passover lamb was unblemished and was slaughtered, and its blood on the doorposts turned away the destroyer. Christ is called our Passover, and believers were redeemed with the precious blood of a lamb without blemish or spot, 1 Peter 1:18-19. In Revelation the Lamb's blood is not a sign on a doorpost but the price that purchases a people. It is more than the type could be. Each Passover lamb covered one household for a night; the Lamb who was slain has bought people from every nation, for good.

At Sinai God promised that Israel, if it kept His covenant, would be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The song of verse 10 says that the Lamb has made the redeemed to be this. Peter applies the same words to the church, 1 Peter 2:9. The correspondence is the calling to serve God and stand before Him on behalf of others. It is enlarged by the Lamb's work, since the people are no longer one nation but a multitude from all nations, and they have been made priests by purchase and not by their own obedience.

typology.type: The prayers of the saints as incense, Psalm 141:2
typology.fulfillment: David asked that his prayer be set before God like incense. In Revelation 5:8 the elders hold golden bowls full of incense, and John tells us that these are the prayers of the saints. In 8:3-4 the smoke of the incense rises with the prayers before God. The picture tells us that the prayers of weak believers on earth are valued like temple incense and are in heaven's hands. The correspondence is not a picture of the Lamb but of the church, and it falls short of showing how prayer is received.

study.christ:
This chapter is about Christ more directly than any other in the book. The first thing it shows is His worthiness. The question 'Who is worthy?' is not answered by a list of qualities. It is answered by a Person, and the Person is identified by what He did: 'You were slain.' His worthiness does not rest on strength alone, nor on position alone, but on the cross. Everything John learns about Jesus in the rest of the book will be seen in this light.

It shows Him as a king and as a sacrifice at once. The Lion of Judah fulfils Genesis 49:9-10, and the Root of David fulfils Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10. Yet the sight is a Lamb. The two do not contradict one another. John is told that the Lion 'has triumphed' and shown how: by being the Lamb who was slain. The cross is not the prelude to a later victory but the victory itself. That is why the Lamb stands at the centre of the throne and why, in Revelation 6 and the chapters after, it is the Lamb who opens the seals.

It shows Him as the one who is alive. The Lamb 'appeared to have been slain,' yet He is standing. The cross happened and its marks remain, and the resurrection means that He lives. His presence in the middle of the throne also shows that He reigns. In 3:21 He promised the overcomer a seat on His throne, and here He is seen with the Father.

It shows Him as the one to whom worship is given. The song of the creatures and the elders is addressed to the Lamb, and the doxology of verse 13 is addressed jointly to the One on the throne and to the Lamb. John 5:23 says that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father, and Philippians 2:9-11 says that every knee will bow at the name of Jesus. This is an early statement in the New Testament of His deity, and it is made in the very place where Jewish monotheism is most carefully guarded, the throne room.

It shows Him as the one who purchased a people. 'By Your blood You purchased for God' is the language of Acts 20:28, where the church is purchased with His own blood, and of Revelation 1:5-6, where He freed us by His blood and made us a kingdom of priests. The cost of the purchase is His own life.

It shows Him as the Lord of the Spirit, since the seven eyes are the Spirit sent out into all the earth. The Lamb's work is applied in the world by the Spirit.

A caution is in order. The seven horns and the seven eyes are not to be read as a puzzle of numbers. They say that He has complete power and complete knowledge. The details of the scene serve one claim: the slain Lamb is worthy of the throne.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the sovereign who holds the future in His hand. The scroll is in His right hand, the hand of power and authority, and no one takes it from Him. He is not shown struggling to complete His purposes. The crisis in verses 2 to 4 is not that God's plan is uncertain but that the plan needs a worthy agent, and the answer is that God Himself provides one. As Abraham said, 'God Himself will provide the lamb,' Genesis 22:8.

He is the God who gives to the Lamb. The Father places the scroll in His hand, and the Lamb takes it. This is a scene of shared rule in which the Father hands over the carrying out of His plan to the Son. It tells us that the God of the Bible is not a solitary monarch but a communion, and that the plan of redemption is the shared work of Father, Son and Spirit.

He is the God who saves at great cost. The song says the Lamb purchased people for God, and the price was blood. The God of Revelation does not rescue cheaply. He does not simply declare the guilty forgiven. He provides a sacrifice from within His own life, and the Lamb is the God-given way.

He is the God of all nations. The redeemed come from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. That the nations are His is no new idea. He had promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed, and the Psalmist asked that the nations be given as an inheritance, Psalm 2:8. But here the promise is seen as accomplished.

He is the God who answers prayers. The bowls of incense are the prayers of the saints, and they are held in heaven. It is a quiet, moving detail, and it says that no prayer is lost.

He is the God who is worshiped by all creation. In verse 13 every creature, in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, praises both the One on the throne and the Lamb. There is no neutral part of the universe left. The God who made all things is acknowledged by all things.

There is a tension that the passage holds with care. God is the one who rules from the throne, and yet the way He saves is by the Lamb's weakness. His power is not the power of the lion alone. The chapter teaches that God's strength is shown in a love that gives itself up, and worship that does not see this has not yet understood Him.

crossReferences.note: Jacob blesses Judah as a young lion whose scepter will not depart until the one to whom it belongs comes and the nations obey Him. The elder's announcement of the Lion of the tribe of Judah is this promise, and the scene shows how it is fulfilled.

A shoot comes from the stump of Jesse, a Branch from his roots. The picture of a cut-down line springing up again fills out the title Root of David in verse 5, and it ties the Lamb's slain and risen life to the hope of David's house.

On that day the Root of Jesse stands as a banner for the peoples, and the nations seek Him. In Revelation 5 the nations are indeed gathered to Him, brought by His blood, which is the surprising way this prophecy comes about.

The servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open His mouth. The slain Lamb of Revelation 5:6 stands in this tradition, and the silent sufferer of Isaiah is the same figure who now stands at the centre of the throne.

The seven eyes of the LORD scan the whole earth. Revelation 5:6 says the seven eyes of the Lamb are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth, tying the Lamb to the LORD's own watching presence in the world.

Ezekiel is given a scroll written on the front and back with words of lamentation, mourning and woe. The writing on both sides in Revelation 5:1 recalls it, and it suggests a scroll heavy with judgment as well as promise.

One like the Son of Man is led to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom for all peoples. The Lamb's approach to the throne and the taking of the scroll is the New Testament form of the same scene.
Daniel is told to seal up the words until the time of the end. The sealed scroll of Revelation 5 recalls this command. What was shut up until the end is now opened by the one who alone has the right.

John the Baptist points to Jesus and says, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' The title of Revelation 5 is already a title of the Gospel, and the one who takes away sin is the one who opens the scroll.

Believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot. The language of purchase in Revelation 5:9 draws on the same understanding of the price paid.

Jesus is the faithful witness, the one who has released us from our sins by His blood and made us a kingdom, priests to His God and Father. The song of Revelation 5:9-10 repeats this and shows heaven singing what the opening doxology says.

A multitude too large to count from every nation, tribe, people and tongue stands before the throne and the Lamb and cries out for salvation. It is the fulfilment of the purchase in 5:9, shown as the crowd that has been gathered.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The Lamb who took the scroll at the centre of the throne is seen at the end of the book as the source of life in the new creation.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a good creation and a human race commissioned to rule it, Genesis 1:26-28. The fall turns that rule into rebellion and puts humanity under the power of death. From then on, the Scriptures are one long search for a human being who can do what Adam failed to do and who can also deal with what he did. A scroll that no one can open is the shape of that problem. Creation has a purpose and a destiny, but no creature is able to carry it out.

The prophets promised such a person in several forms. Jacob spoke of a lion from Judah. Isaiah promised a Root from Jesse. Daniel saw one like a son of man who received dominion. Isaiah saw a suffering servant led like a lamb. God told Abraham He would provide the lamb. The Old Testament never joined these figures. A king who conquers and a servant who is slain seemed to belong to different stories. Revelation 5 is the moment when they are shown to be one Person. The Lion is the Lamb.

The chapter also answers the exile from Eden and the failure of Israel. The people who were meant to be a kingdom of priests had broken the covenant. The Lamb's purchase makes a new people, drawn from every nation, who are what Israel was called to be. In Genesis 12:3 God promised that all families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, and in Revelation 5:9 that promise is reaching its goal.

The scene also sets in motion the rest of the book. Once the Lamb opens the scroll, the history of the world moves towards its end, and the judgments of chapters 6 to 16 are the Lamb's. The final chapters follow with the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, and the new Jerusalem, where the throne of God and of the Lamb stands in the city and His servants worship Him and see His face, Revelation 22:3-4. The song that begins with a few voices in chapter 5 swells there to include every creature, and the curse is no more. The creation that no one could unlock is finally opened, and what is inside is the glory of God.

sermon.title: Lamb on the Throne
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly on Revelation 5:1-14, tracing the sealed scroll, the search for one worthy, and the Lamb's triumph through sacrifice, drawing out the sweeping scope of the redemption purchased for every tribe, tongue, and nation, which is the exact center of this section.

quiz.q: Why does John weep in the opening scene of chapter 5?

options.text: No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth was found worthy to open the sealed scroll.
options.note: Verses 3-4 give this exact reason for his grief.

options.text: Because the Lamb had not yet been slain.
options.note: The Lamb's death has already occurred; John weeps because no one was found worthy to open the scroll, not because the sacrifice was still future.

options.text: Because the twenty-four elders refused to worship.
options.note: The elders are shown worshiping throughout; that is not the cause of John's weeping.

options.text: Because the throne room had gone silent forever.
options.note: The throne room is filled with sound and song throughout; John weeps over the scroll remaining unopened.

quiz.q: What does John see when he looks for the Lion of the tribe of Judah?

options.text: A Lamb standing as though slain, at the center of the throne, who takes the scroll.
options.note: Verses 6-7 describe exactly this reversal of expectation.

options.text: A literal lion standing beside the throne.
options.note: The lion language is titular; what John actually sees is a Lamb, not a literal lion.

options.text: An empty throne with no one able to approach it.
options.note: The Lamb does approach and does take the scroll from the One on the throne.

options.text: One of the twenty-four elders taking the scroll himself.
options.note: An elder announces the Lion's triumph, but it is the Lamb, not an elder, who takes the scroll.

quiz.q: On what basis is the Lamb declared worthy in the new song of verse 9?

options.text: Because He was slain and by His blood purchased people for God from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.
options.note: Verse 9 states this exact ground for His worthiness.

options.text: Because He created all things.
options.note: That was the ground for the Father's worthiness in chapter 4; the Lamb's worthiness here rests on redemption, not creation.

options.text: Because He defeated the beast in open battle.
options.note: No such battle has yet occurred in the narrative; His worthiness rests on His sacrificial death.

options.text: Because the elders chose Him by vote.
options.note: His worthiness is declared as an already established fact grounded in His blood, not decided by a vote.

quiz.q: What happens to the scope of worship as the chapter unfolds?

options.text: It widens from the four living creatures and elders, to countless angels, to every creature in all creation.
options.note: Verses 8-13 trace exactly this widening circle of worship.

options.text: It remains limited to the twenty-four elders alone throughout the chapter.
options.note: The elders participate throughout, but the worship expands far beyond them to angels and all creation.

options.text: It fades away once the Lamb takes the scroll.
options.note: The opposite occurs; worship grows louder and wider after the Lamb takes the scroll.

options.text: It is restricted only to beings in heaven, excluding earth and sea.
options.note: Verse 13 explicitly includes every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea.

quiz.q: What does the Lamb's purchase accomplish for those from every tribe and nation, according to verse 10?

options.text: It makes them a kingdom and priests to God, destined to reign.
options.note: Verse 10 states this exact outcome of the Lamb's redemptive purchase.

options.text: It merely rescues them from physical danger on earth.
options.note: The purchase includes far more than physical rescue; it constitutes them as a kingdom and priesthood before God.

options.text: It exempts them from ever facing tribulation.
options.note: Revelation elsewhere shows the redeemed enduring tribulation; the purchase secures their identity and destiny, not exemption from all hardship.

options.text: It has no lasting effect beyond the moment of the song.
options.note: The song describes a permanent, established reality: a purchased kingdom and priesthood destined to reign.

questions: John wept because no one was found worthy to open the scroll, until the Lamb appeared. Where in your life do you need to remember that Christ alone, not your own effort, is worthy to bring God's purposes to pass?

The Lion of Judah turned out to be a slaughtered Lamb; His triumph came through sacrifice, not despite it. Where are you tempted to measure victory by worldly strength rather than by costly, sacrificial love?
The Lamb's blood purchased people from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation. How does this shape the way you see and love people who are different from you?

Heaven's worship widened from the inner circle to countless angels to every creature in creation. What would it look like for your own worship of Christ to grow wider and louder rather than staying small and private?
The redeemed are made a kingdom and priests, destined to reign. How does knowing your ultimate destiny is to reign with Christ change how you face today's struggles and disappointments?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote allows 'the sevenfold Spirit' as an alternate rendering for 'the seven Spirits of God,' the same fullness-of-the-Spirit imagery used already in Revelation 1:4 and 4:5, here tied directly to the Lamb who sends the Spirit into all the earth.

The BSB footnote notes the Greek can be read 'they will reign over' or, following the Westcott-Hort text, the present tense 'they reign upon,' a manuscript question that affects whether the saints' reign is depicted as already begun or entirely future.
The Textus Receptus adds the phrase 'Him who lives for ever and ever' to the elders' closing worship in some manuscript traditions, though the shorter reading is well attested and used here.
